data.title: The 50 percent problem with Trump's Canada tariffs
data.description:
President Trump recently used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 as the legal basis for his new trade war on Canada, imposing 50 percent tariffs on some $20 billion in goods that the U.S. imports annually, covering everything from hockey sticks to alcohol. 

But “up to 50 percent” does not mean 50 percent whenever the president feels like it. And it doesn’t mean any form of alleged discrimination. Congress passed Section 338 to give the president a tool to retaliate against foreign countries that discriminated against the U.S. in tariffs and other customs matters, not against any practice that the government deems unfair. These distinctions could become important when Trump’s new tariffs on Canada invariably end up in court.

The Federal Circuit Court’s decision in HMTX Industries v. U.S. explains why. Importers challenged the massive expansion of the tariffs Trump imposed on China in his first term under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. If the administration could turn an initial $50 billion trade action into tariffs covering more than $350 billion in imports, they asked, what prevented this provision from authorizing an all-out trade war?

The Federal Circuit rejected that argument. The U.S. Trade Representative’s power was not limitless, the court explained, because any modified tariff remained tied to the original action and had to be tailored to the statutory goal of eliminating the Chinese conduct under investigation. It could not raise tariffs “for any reason” or by an amount that wasn’t “appropriate” to achieve its original goal.

Those limiting principles should matter under Section 338. In July, Trump stated that Canadian measures involving automobiles, dairy and alcoholic beverages discriminated against American exports of cars, cheese and booze. 

Take the case of automobiles. The proclamation says that Canadian discrimination denies American car makers export opportunities, along with the economic benefits that come from selling more cars to Canada. Yet it also says the tariffs will expand opportunities for U.S. car makers to sell more cars at home, increase domestic production and employment, and “may spur Canada to remove the discrimination.”

These are not the same objectives. Compensating for a loss of export markets is remedial. Protecting American producers from Canadian competition is protectionist. Imposing enough economic pain to make Ottawa change its policies is coercive. 

Section 338 may grant wide latitude in designing a remedy. But Congress chose the word “offset.” And the definition of the word at the time was clear, as it is today. As the Merriam-Webster dictionary defines it, to “offset” something is “to counterbalance or to compensate for something else.” This limits the president to imposing tariffs in an amount and on those products that will compensate for the burden Canada’s discrimination places on U.S. companies.

But the White House’s own figures put the alleged lost exports at $5.6 billion for autos and $582 million for alcohol, nowhere near the $20 billion in goods subject to Trump’s 50 percent tariffs. And cars and car parts are not on the list of products subject to tariffs, begging the question of how these tariffs are supposed to protect American car producers from Canadian competition.

HMTX suggests courts should be skeptical of precisely this move to impose tariffs in any amount, on any product, for any reason the president wants. The court did not hold that once U.S. Trade Representative found an actionable Chinese practice, it acquired a general tariff power over China.

Suppose Canada adopted a measure costing American exporters $500 million annually. Could the president respond with $10 billion in tariffs on unrelated Canadian products because doing so might force Ottawa to surrender?

A statutory maximum tells the president how far he can go if the facts support a maximum tariff. It does not tell him how far he should go in any particular case. Rather, Congress instructed the president to offset the burden or disadvantage of a particular type of discriminatory action. That requires some demonstrable relationship between the injury and the remedy.

Trump’s decision to go directly to the statutory maximum makes that question especially important. Why does a 50 percent tariff offset the Canadian disadvantage when 15 or 25 percent would not? Simply repeating the statutory word “offset” does not answer those questions. 

That is the important lesson of HMTX. The federal circuit rejected the specter of a “limitless trade war” precisely because Section 301’s remedial purpose continued to constrain the tariffs imposed under it. The same logic should apply to any attempt to use Section 338. 

If 50 percent represents what is necessary to offset a demonstrated Canadian disadvantage, Trump has a statutory argument. If, instead, it simply represents the amount of pressure Trump picked to prosecute the newest of his many trade wars, then something fundamentally different has happened.

Marc L. Busch is the Karl F. Landegger Professor of International Business Diplomacy at the Walsh School of Foreign Service, Georgetown University. Peter E. Harrell is a visiting scholar at Georgetown’s Institute of International Economic Law and attorney in private practice. Jennifer Hillman is a professor from Practice at the Georgetown University Law Center.

data.title: Hawley expands Flock camera probe to other AI-powered surveillance systems
data.description:
GOP Sen. Josh Hawley (Mo.) announced Thursday he would broaden his probe into Flock Safety’s roadside cameras to include AI surveillance networks run by three other companies. 

“Flock does not stand alone in the surveillance industry,” the senator, who serves as the chair of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, wrote on social media.

“Other companies are also building large camera networks, assisted by artificial intelligence, that intrude on the privacy of all Americans,” he continued. “That is why I’m expanding my investigation.”

In new letters to the top executives of Motorola Solutions Inc., Verkada Inc. and Axon Enterprise Inc., Hawley requested information about these companies’ policies around the retention and use of citizen data collected by their AI camera networks. 

The Hill has reached out to all three companies for comment. 

Last week, the Missouri lawmaker wrote to Flock CEO Garrett Langley, expressing concerns that the company’s network of more than 120,000 cameras across 49 states has led to “abuse and misuse of personal data” because of a “woeful lack of safeguards in these systems.”

The company has faced public outcry amid reports that police officers across the nation have abused the nationwide surveillance network to spy on former romantic partners. Several police departments have severed their contracts with the company due to concerns about a lack of safeguards.

GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.) unveiled the “Flock-Off Act” in the House this week, which would block the use of federal funding for automated license plate reader cameras and biometric surveillance cameras. 

“The federal government shouldn’t provide ‘security’ grants to cities and police departments that have gone beyond the pale and turned their communities into a version of ‘1984,’” the Kentucky Republican said in a press release.

Flock criticized the House bill in a statement to The Hill on Thursday, warning it could “have real consequences for public safety.”

“Rather than banning a critical public safety tool, Congress should consider strong, clear safeguards that ensure accountability, oversight, and responsible use are enshrined in law,” a company spokesperson said. “We do not have to choose between protecting privacy and giving law enforcement the tools it needs to keep communities safe. We can — and should — do both.”

data.title: Lindsay Clancy judge, defense attorney spar over holdout juror
data.description:
(NewsNation) – The judge in the Lindsay Clancy trial will not have a private hearing with a holdout juror, he told attorneys Friday in a heated exchange with the defense. He also said future notes from the jury should refrain from mentioning the status of deliberations.

The jury was then sent off for a seventh day of deliberations Friday morning.

Judge William Sullivan decided not to remove the juror after defense attorney Kevin Reddington said the juror should be booted for refusing to follow instructions on reasonable doubt.

He instead said the jury would again be reminded of their duties, stating he had read them the instructions on how to come to a decision beyond “reasonable doubt.”

Reddington called Sullivan’s reading of those jury instructions “soft” and asked the judge to do it more “forcefully.”

“What do you want me to do? Get a brass band?” Sullivan said in the heated exchange.

Jury indicated one juror was holding out; defense says they’re not listening to the law

In Thursday’s proceedings, a note was sent to Sullivan in the Lindsay Clancy trial, indicating 11 of the 12 jurors had decided on a verdict, with only one juror holding out, according to Reddington.

NOW PLAYING

A heated sidebar ensued between Reddington and Sullivan.

Reddington reportedly waved papers and slammed his hands down, but what was said in the exchange is not known.

Afterward, Clancy was wheeled over to the bench as Sullivan, prosecutors and her lawyer gathered while jurors were called one by one to the bench. Sullivan spoke with each juror, who were sworn in inches from Clancy.

Reddington called for the dismissal of the holdout juror and argued that the note indicated the juror was not applying the judge’s instruction, but Sullivan refused.

“I don’t feel it’s proper for me to side with one side or the other of the deliberations,” Sullivan said.

Sullivan questioned the jurors individually before bringing the panel out to the jury box. The jury was sent to deliberate and was later dismissed without a verdict.

Lindsay Clancy’s attorney wants everything in open court

On Friday, Reddington filed an emergency motion demanding an end to sidebar conversations and instead have the rest of the trial communications take place in open court.

Clancy’s trial has taken place on camera and has been broadcast across news stations and online.

What will happen if a mistrial is declared in the Lindsay Clancy case?

If Sullivan declares a mistrial, prosecutors will decide whether to try Clancy again, pursue a plea deal or drop the charges.

On Wednesday, after two days in a deadlock, Sullivan read jurors the Tuey-Rodriguez instruction, also known as a “dynamite charge,” a Massachusetts law that instructs jurors to assess their own views and those opposing without dismissing their own honestly held beliefs. State law says a judge cannot send the jury back to deliberate a third time without their consent, unless they ask the court for further explanation of the law.

The jury has spent six days and over 35 hours deliberating. The prosecution argues Clancy knew what she was doing when she killed her three kids in 2023. The defense argues she was in the grips of postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible.

data.title: The war on women is happening in a warehouse, not in the statehouse
data.description:
The next front in the fight for the rights of American women is not in the doctor’s office. It’s in an Amazon fulfillment warehouse and a Speedway convenience store. That’s where working-class women in shift and hourly jobs, the backbone of the American economy, suffer systematic abuses that may get worse pending the results of this year’s midterm elections.

That’s because policy decisions that deeply affect millions of working women will be finalized this November as American voters cast ballots grading President Trump’s second term.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, an under-the-radar government agency created decades ago to protect women and minorities against unfair workplace measures, is being hollowed out from within as, in the administration’s words, a place for white men to report perceived abuses.

The commission announced late last month that it will finalize new proposed policy regulations within days of the elections, including undoing decades of workplace policy advances that allowed women to balance work and family.

Among other destructive line items, it is anticipated that new policy measures will essentially negate the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, a bipartisan law signed in 2022 that ensured basic workplace accommodations for pregnant and postpartum women. These accommodations are often remarkably modest: access to water, temporary lifting restrictions, bathroom breaks, a chair during the third trimester, time off for prenatal treatments or fertility procedures or space to pump breast milk.

But unmaking these measures will result in systematically pushing women out of the workplace. And that’s exactly what they are intended to do, whether it is freshly emboldened, multibillion-dollar mega-corporations seeking to automate or fringe religious activists long eager to turn back the clock on women exiting the home to endter the workforce.    

The women most affected are not executives or professionals with college degrees and jobs with typically generous leave and accommodations policies. The women most affected will be warehouse pickers, cashiers and factory workers who cannot work from home or absorb months without a paycheck, who desperately depend on their $20 per hour wages.  

Consider the story of an Amazon warehouse associate with a high-risk pregnancy who reached out to my organization. Despite doctors’ orders, Amazon refused her basic accommodations, including sitting breaks. She was repeatedly hospitalized before ultimately losing her job.

A pregnant Speedway cashier who reached out to us was likewise denied the ability to sit while working. She suffered a pregnancy-related medical emergency and was forced onto involuntary, unpaid leave.

These changes at the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission are not occurring in isolation. They fit within a broader agenda that increasingly seeks to push women toward motherhood and away from economic independence. Trump has considered numerous such proposals — including birthing bonuses and even a “national medal of motherhood” for women with six or more children. 

It is not just a regressive concept of societal roles. Passing the SAVE Act would also make it more difficult for millions of women to vote, and the Department of Health and Human Services is undermining comprehensive reproductive health care and advancing a narrow vision of women’s health centered on childbirth. 

Few of these developments have entered the national conversation, which is likely by design. The affected women are largely working-class and fearful of losing a paycheck. They cannot afford legal teams, lobbyists and communications specialists. 

My organization’s free legal helpline hears from thousands of workers each year with similar stories. Their pleas are not political, but practical. Can they keep their jobs while pregnant? Can they return to work after having a baby? Can they continue supporting their families without being forced to choose between their health and their paycheck?  

These questions go to the heart of whether the nation’s economy can include women, and whether the concept of opportunity means anything at all if women can be pushed out of the workforce because it serves a radical political ideology.

In four months, millions of Americans will head to the polls. The same month, a federal agency will take a massive step toward allowing the firing of millions of American women, permanently altering the independence of women across the country.

If there is no accountability for this incoming economic and social disaster, it will be because we let it happen. And, in doing so, we would reveal that the women who pack our deliveries and swipe our cards after we fill up the car just aren’t very important to some people.   

Inimai Chettiar is the president of A Better Balance, an advocate for paid leave, family leave and workplace policy advancements for women and families.

data.title: Former podcaster charged for death threats against Trump
data.description:
Former podcaster Benjamin Azariah Southworth was charged Thursday in connection with death threats against President Trump.

FBI Director Kash Patel announced Southworth was arrested in a statement on the social platform X, writing, “Early this morning, the @FBI and partners arrested Benjamin Azariah Southworth in LA – after a federal grand jury indicted him for allegedly threatening to assassinate President Trump and his attorney, Jay Sekulow.”

“Deadly threats like this are as vile as they are criminal – those responsible will be met by this FBI and law enforcement,” Patel added.

The grand jury indictment found Southworth used his social media — including his Instagram, YouTube and Tiktok — to “publicly engage in and/or encourage the abuse, harassment and intimidation of, and violence against, President Trump.”

The second victim was not identified in the indictment but was described as “President Trump’s personal lawyer and that lawyer’s family.”

Southworth is the former host of the podcast “Yass, Jesus!” and a Christian reality show called “The Remix.”

Prosecutors cited as evidence one video Southworth posted in April where he reportedly made death threats against the president and portrayed “fictitious portrayals of acts of violence” against Trump. 

Southworth allegedly posted in April on his social platforms, “IF AT FIRST YOU FAIL, TRY AGAIN!” following a shooting at the White House Correspondent’s Dinner.

Three months before these posts, prosecutors said Southworth also posted Sekulow’s home address along with his picture on his personal Tiktok account with a statement that read, “No peace for traitors.”

He is charged with cyberstalking and harassing Sekulow and threatening to kill Trump.

“As threats against President Trump’s life escalate, the Department of Justice will respond with the full force of the law,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a press release. “We will hold perpetrators of violent threats accountable, and anyone who makes these threats online will not be allowed to hide behind their screens.”

The case is still under investigation. If convicted, Southworth would face a statutory maximum sentence of five years in federal prison for threatening the president, a statutory maximum sentence of five years in federal prison for cyberstalking and a statutory maximum sentence of two years in federal prison for telephonic harassment.

data.title: India-France ties should not replace relations with Washington
data.description:
On its face, France and India do not have much in common. France is a NATO ally; India has remained outside any alliance system. France had numerous colonies around the world and maintains relations with many of them since they achieved independence. India was not one of those countries — it was the jewel in the British crown. 

Yet both states have a common self-perception as independent poles in a multipolar world.

Despite its membership of NATO, France’s long-standing refusal to join NATO’s nuclear planning group reflects both its determination to maintain the independence of its nuclear deterrent and policy of what president Emmanuel Macron calls “strategic autonomy.” And he is extending a French nuclear umbrella to other European states.

India, like France, is a nuclear power. It too has long pursued an independent national security policy. New Delhi did have close military and economic relations with the Soviet Union and still is a major purchaser of Russian oil. Nevertheless, the former leader of the non-aligned group of nations has no formal alliances and does not seek any. 

Although France and India have maintained good relations since India achieved independence in 1947, their ties reached a turning point in 1998. That was when India conducted five nuclear tests and Washington issued sanctions against India. France did not. Indeed, France upgraded its strategic relationship with India that year.

Since the turn of the century, France and India have increasingly strengthened their technological, economic and especially military relations. Apart from counterpart visits by leading military and civilian officials, as well as naval visits, the two countries have conducted bilateral naval exercises since 2001; air force exercises since 2003; army exercises since 2011. India has also participated in the French-led multinational Orion exercises.

India has been a market for French armaments. These include India’s 2016 purchase of 36 Rafale aircraft; its 2025 acquisition of 26 Rafale-M fighters for its aircraft carriers; and a 2026 additional purchase of 114 Rafale fighters. In addition, in 2005 India purchased designs for six French Scorpene submarines that it built domestically. India has recently ordered three more submarines from France.

Last year the French Directorate General of Armaments and the Indian DefenseResearch and Development Organization signed a broad-based agreement to deepen their  collaboration. This included, among other areas, “aeronautical platforms, unmanned vehicles, advanced materials… cyber security, artificial intelligence … advanced sensors … [and] underwater technologies.” The agreement built upon a long-term strategic plan that the two countries formulated in 2023, termed Horizon 2047.

Finally, after an exchange of visits by French president Emmanuel Macron and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and on the recommendation of India’s parliamentary standing committee on defense, New Delhi and Paris began discussions last month on Indian participation in the French Future Combat Air System that will develop a sixth generation fighter.

In contrast with their deepening mutual relations, both countries not only have had a historically uneasy relationship with Washington, but they also have a common apprehension  about the direction that American national security and economic policies have taken. France, as a member of the European Union, constantly lives under the shadow of new American tariffs imposed on EU products, or those that it produces on its own.

For example, in June, President Trump threatened to hit the French wine industry with a 100 percent tariff if it did not drop its digital services tax on American technology companies. Whether he will make good on that threat is unclear, but French apprehension should come as no surprise.

India also faces the threat of American tariffs. In early September the Senate passed the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia Act that imposes a 100 percent tariff on the five leading importers of Russian oil. India is one of them. The legislation is stalled in the House, but it could pass during the lame-duck period after the November elections.

Both countries also have recent grievances regarding American policies. France lost its sale of Barracuda submarines to Australia because of the AUKUS agreement, which provided for a British-American solution to Canberra’s requirement for new submarines. India, ever suspicious of Pakistan, has resented Washington’s reliance upon Islamabad as a go-between in Washington’s on-again off-again negotiations with Iran. 

Like other states, notably in the Middle East, Paris and New Delhi are jointly hedging their bets against what they perceive might be future American policies. That is not an outcome that will benefit the U.S. France’s policy of extending its deterrent umbrella should complement the American deterrent, not replace it.

As an increasingly powerful player in Asia, India should work alongside, rather than apart from, Washington’s efforts to deter an increasingly aggressive China. There is much to be said for the blossoming French-Indian partnership, but it should not come about because of a loss of faith in American reliability.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

data.title: Ty Cobb on midterms: Trump intends 'to steal these elections where possible'
data.description:
Former Trump White House lawyer Ty Cobb said Thursday that President Trump would attempt to “steal” the 2026 midterm elections “where possible.”

Cobb, in an appearance on MS NOW Thursday, discussed reports of GOP lawmakers declining to attend a Republican National Committee event, underlining concerns about Trump’s political brand almost two years into his second term.

A source familiar told The Hill that the National Republican Congressional Committee distributed more than 2,000 tickets for the convention and that around 100 members and candidates were confirmed to attend. Lawmakers are expected to contribute a minimum $25,000 to take part.

“Well, I think the Republicans who are saying no are being strategic,” Cobb said. “But at the same time, he’s [Trump] sitting on $400 million in campaign money that he could donate to some of these elections. And he’s not.”

Cobb added that, “It also plays into a narrative that I think people are undervaluing, which is I think Trump doesn’t feel he needs to spend this money because it is his intention to interfere with the elections and to steal these elections where possible.”

He raised the possibility that Trump could “urge” House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to refuse to swear in Democratic candidates following the midterm elections. Johnson was an active backer of Trump’s efforts to overturn his 2020 election loss to former President Biden.

The Trump administration is still pushing to restrict mail-in voting for the midterms, even as states start sending out early ballots. The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to allow for the U.S. Postal Service’s (USPS) implementation of Trump’s executive order targeting mail voting. 

USPS’s plan would mandate that states’ mail-in ballots meet design requirements — such as unique barcodes and an official logo — and require election officials to upload lists of voters who are eligible to vote by mail. If a ballot doesn’t meet the specifications or someone is not on the submitted list, USPS would refuse to deliver it. 

In a July appearance on MS NOW, Cobb argued that moves from Trump like this are rooted in his refusal to accept his 2020 defeat.

“The most grievous thing that ever happened to him was he lost an election,” he said at the time. “As a malignant narcissist, he just can’t abide that.”

data.title: Diesel prices hit record high
data.description:
The average price of diesel hit an all-time high Friday in the U.S., as the conflict with Iran puts more strain on the global energy supply.

The average cost of a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was up to around $5.85 on Friday morning, according to AAA. This is a 58 percent cost increase from a year ago, when a gallon of diesel was around $3.71 on average, and nearly a 9 percent increase from last month, when a gallon was about $5.37 on average. 

In addition to higher transportation costs, rising diesel prices are likely to push up the price of everyday goods, since the fuel is commonly used by commercial delivery trucks. 

This marks the latest blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to downplay the domestic economic costs of the war with Iran in the lead up to the midterm elections. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a major oil trading corridor, during the turmoil has strained global crude oil supplies. 

In June, President Trump directed the Justice Department (DOJ) to open an investigation into alleged gas price gouging as his approval rating took a hit amid rising fuel costs. A July poll from The Associated Press and NORC Research Center found that 66 percent of respondents disapproved of how the president is handling the U.S. economy. 

In a Friday morning statement shared with The Hill, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said the president “remains committed to unleashing American energy dominance” and reducing costs. 

“This week the President met with nearly a dozen refiners to discuss ways to expand our refining capacity, which will lower prices at the pump,” Rogers continued. “As the U.S. military fully degrades the terrorist Iranian regime’s ability to attack shipping vessels, oil and gas prices will fall back to pre-conflict levels.”

The price for standard gas has also been on the rise during the Iran war, which has now stretched into a sixth month. The average price of regular gas was around $4.18 per gallon on Friday, up from about $3.20 a gallon last year, according to AAA. 

In August, fuel rate tracker GasBuddy found that standard gas prices were the highest they had ever been this late in the year. The group’s top petroleum analyst, Patrick De Haan, said the national average of regular gas had never exceeded $4 a gallon after Aug. 12 in any previous year.

data.title: ICE's new 'shock gloves' are dangerous, inhumane and totally unnecessary
data.description:
According to a recent Department of Homeland Security notice, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency plans to spend up to $20 million on gloves that deliver painful electric shocks. At the push of a button, a one-second shock from these gloves can send a grown man to the ground.

On “Fox & Friends,” White House border czar Tom Homan said the gloves would prevent ICE agents from needing to use deadly force. “It’s another device to help someone get compliant when they are not.”

These shock gloves are a new low in ICE’s campaign of cruelty. Their use holds great potential for harm to migrants and U.S. citizens alike, and will enable more ICE brutality while helping agents evade accountability for their actions.

The manufacturer of the gloves, formally named the Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, markets them as a “de-escalation device.” But there is no reason to believe that ICE agents will use them that way. Instead, the gloves will likely embolden a paramilitary force known for aggressive behavior, racial profiling and violence.

ICE agents have kicked, punched and tackled people hundreds of times, and deployed chemical irritants regularly. They use chokeholds and neck restraints, tactics that are prohibited by other law enforcement agencies. They have fatally shot at least three confirmed American citizens: Alex Pretti, Renee Good and Ruben Ray Martinez. With the shock gloves, agents will have a new tool with which to inflict pain on anyone they say is suspected of being in the country illegally.  

The manufacturer of the shock gloves warns that they should not be used on children, pregnant woman, the elderly or disabled people. Yet ICE frequently encounters members of these high-risk categories. People with disabilities are especially vulnerable to harm from the gloves, because not all medical conditions — like epilepsy, heart disease or mental health issues — are visible. Given that ICE disproportionately targets Latinos, a demographic with high rates of cardiovascular disease, the planned use of the gloves will almost certainly lead to serious medical incidents.

Consider that the gloves’ training manual comes with a red warning label, noting that improper use may result in injury or death.

The rationale behind the use of such gloves is disturbing. They were specifically designed to be “low optics,” meaning their use will not be visible as other policing methods. On a promotional video by the manufacturer, supporters of the gloves say that they “Look better to those witnesses” and that they are “conducive to not leading to lawsuits.” Because the electric shocks do not leave burns or marks, there is nothing to stop agents from using the gloves repeatedly on a person, or after a person has been subdued. Nor is there anything to prevent multiple agents from shocking a single person simultaneously. What could possibly go wrong?

The real question is why ICE needs these gloves at all. Immigration agents are well equipped with firearms, pepper spray and batons. ICE and the Customs and Border Protection agency plan to spend $144 million in 2025 on guns, ammunition and “less lethal” weapons such as tasers and pepper sprays, according to a February report by Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.). Just weeks later, the administration announced its intent to purchase more than 17,000 tasers for another $220 million. It’s hard to see how agents need another tool in their arsenal when they are already armed to the hilt.

ICE’s shock gloves raise legal issues as well. Their use may violate the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition of “cruel and unusual punishment,” and the constitutional guarantee of due process. New York’s governor and attorney general have both criticized the new gloves, suggesting that their use may run afoul of state and civil rights laws.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said, “ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country.” Yet ICE is generally not going after “criminal illegal aliens.” About 70 percent of people in immigration detention have no criminal convictions at all. ICE is also operating in an environment with little oversight, as the administration has gutted the agency’s internal watchdogs.

Meanwhile, the president’s popularity is cratering, and a majority of American voters disapprove of how ICE is doing its job. Immigration agents should be reined in, not empowered to inflict more suffering on their targets.

ICE’s shock gloves are dangerous, inhumane and unnecessary. A rogue agency that violates human and civil rights does not deserve more weapons.

Raul A. Reyes is an award-winning journalist, attorney and television commentator in New York City.

data.title: EPA proposes to further narrow Clean Water Act protections
data.description:
The Trump administration on Friday proposed further narrowing protections under the Clean Water Act.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and Army Corps of Engineers issued a supplemental proposed rule that they said would be likely to reduce the bodies of water that are under the Clean Water Act’s jurisdiction.

It would be expected to reduce the number of waters subject to the Clean Water Act in the West.

That means development or pollution in these bodies of water would no longer require a permit or potential mitigation.

The new changes come on top of an already proposed rule by the agencies that is also expected to narrow the Clean Water Act’s applicability. The additional proposal could narrow it further.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said in a written statement that the agency is aiming to set up a “durable” rule that “follows the law and ends burdensome regulatory uncertainty.”

“Today’s action reflects our continued commitment to transparency and public input, ensuring we have fully considered a wide range of potential policy options. We look forward to public feedback on this supplemental notice, which will help strengthen the real-world expertise behind the final rule,” he said.

DEVELOPING.
